**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Distinguish a parameter, an estimator and an estimate, and explain what a standard error measures. Compare estimators by their bias, efficiency and consistency. Choose a model and an estimation method for your outcome, and interpret its coefficients in the units of the problem. Read a confidence interval and a p-value correctly, and say whether your question is predictive or causal.

## Handouts

[Results critique cards](../handouts/results-claims.qmd)

## Where to read more

[Adams](https://doi.org/10.4135/9788132108498) ch. 11 on descriptive statistics and ch. 12 on correlation and regression.

## Session A · 2:00–3:15

Most projects in this course estimate an unknown parameter: a price premium, an elasticity, a probability, an effect. This session covers how that estimate is obtained from a sample and how its uncertainty is measured. Live simulations from a population with a known mean show the sampling distribution, the standard error, and why the standard error falls with the square root of the sample size. The German tank problem compares three estimators by their bias, efficiency and consistency. The Literary Digest poll opens the cases a larger sample does not fix: bias, dependent observations, little variation in the regressor, and heavy tails. The session then covers models for continuous, binary and count outcomes, and three estimation methods: least squares, maximum likelihood and the method of moments (GMM). It ends with standard errors from formulas and from the bootstrap, a p-value computed by permutation, confidence intervals read against the smallest effect that matters, and the difference between prediction and causal inference.

## Session B · 3:30–4:30

Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did
since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written
down, and handed in with that session's work.

Ten minutes of simulation first, driven from the front. Draw from a world you control. Watch the p-value distribution under the null. Move the sample size and the variation, and watch it shift. Then fit the same world in and out of sample, and watch an excellent-looking model fail on data it has not seen. Nothing to install. Then the cards. Each team gets an analyst who ran something and said something about it, and every one overclaims differently. A count outcome fitted by OLS and predicted below zero. A 0.03% lift called highly significant across two million users. A wide interval called no effect. An elasticity estimated off two price changes in three years. A churn probability of 112%. Work out what they are actually entitled to claim. Then a team is drawn at random to defend that while the room pushes back. The last line on the sheet is the one that matters: is your own project at risk of the same error?

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.

## Motivation

- Most of your projects will involve estimating an unknown parameter.
- You obtain that estimate from the data.
- Your estimate should be critical for a decision maker.
- Today we discuss estimation: how we obtain estimates from a sample, and how we capture their uncertainty.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. Slow.

A parameter is a fixed quantity that describes a population: a price
premium, an elasticity, a probability, a treatment effect. It is never a
column in the dataset. Every project in this room has to estimate one from a
sample, and the reader of the proposal will ask how precise that estimate
is.

Most of the hour runs in simulated populations where the parameter is known
and shown on screen as a red dashed line. That is the only setting in which
you can watch an estimator's behavior. In their projects the parameter is
unknown.
:::

## Parameters your projects might estimate

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}
| Project lead | Parameter to estimate |
|:--|:--|
| What is a water view worth? | The average price premium for a water view, in dollars or percent |
| When a price rises, what do shoppers switch to? | Diversion ratios: the share of lost sales captured by each substitute |
| Does falling foot traffic predict a closure? | The probability of closure within 12 months, given the foot-traffic trend |
| What is a "locally sourced" claim worth? | Willingness to pay for the label, in cents per unit |
| Did PPP loans change small-business survival? | The average effect of a PPP loan on the survival rate, in percentage points |
| Can card spending nowcast a company's earnings? | Next quarter's revenue, and the size of the forecast error |
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}
Leads from the [project ideas](../project-ideas.qmd) page.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Read two or three rows.

The left column is a question a team could choose. The right column is the
parameter that answers it. None of these is observed directly. The water
view premium is estimated from a comparison of thousands of sales. The
willingness to pay is estimated from respondents' choices between products.

Ask each student to identify the parameter in their own project and keep it
in mind for the hour. Every concept today applies to it: which estimator
produces it, what its standard error is, and whether a larger sample would
reduce its error.

The last row is a forecast. A forecast is also an estimate, and its
uncertainty is the forecast error. Section 7 returns to it.
:::

# 1. Estimators and sampling distributions

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. The section uses one simulated population: 10,000 customers
whose monthly spend is known, so the population mean is known.
:::

## The vocabulary of estimation

- **Population**: the full set of units the question is about. All 10,000 customers.
- **Parameter**: a fixed, unknown quantity of the population. Their mean monthly spend.
- **Sample**: the units we observe. 50 customers drawn at random.
- **Estimator**: a rule that assigns a value to every possible sample. The sample mean.
- **Estimate**: the value the estimator takes in the observed sample.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Read the five terms with their examples.

The parameter here is $67.81. It is known only because the population is
simulated.

Map it onto a project. For the water view question, the population is all
house sales in the market, the parameter is the average premium, the sample
is the sales in the dataset, the estimator is the least squares coefficient
on the water-view indicator, and the estimate is the coefficient reported in
the output.

The distinction to stress is between the last two. The estimator is a rule
that could be applied to any sample. The estimate is the value it produced
in the one sample observed.
:::

## Estimates vary across samples

- **Sampling distribution**: the distribution of an estimator across repeated samples.

<div class="m06" data-demo="sampling" data-n="50" style="width:92%;margin:0 auto"></div>

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. The slide the rest of the hour builds on.

The grey histogram is the population: all 10,000 customers. It is fixed and
never changes; only the sample drawn from it does. The solid red line is the
population mean, $67.81. The distribution is right-skewed: most customers
spend under $100 and a few spend several hundred.

Both panels share one axis, so the solid line runs through both. Click "Draw
one sample". Fifty customers are highlighted in red, and the dashed red line
marks their sample mean. The dot drops straight down into the lower panel.
Read the sample mean out. It differs from $67.81.

Solid is the true value, dashed is an estimate. The same convention holds on
every slide.

Click "Draw one sample" again: a different sample, a different estimate.
Then "Draw 10" and "Draw 1,000".

The lower histogram approximates the sampling distribution of the sample
mean. Three features. Its mean is at the population mean, so the estimator
is unbiased. It has a standard deviation of about $7, which is the next
slide. And on the shared axis it is far narrower than the population: the
mean of 50 customers varies much less than one customer's spend.

In a project you observe one sample and one estimate. The sampling
distribution is never observed. The simulation shows the distribution that
single estimate was drawn from.
:::

## The standard error measures sampling variability

- **Standard error**: the standard deviation of an estimator's sampling distribution.
- Sample mean: σ/√n, where σ is the population standard deviation ($49.02 here).
- Estimated by s/√n, where s is the sample standard deviation.

<div class="m06" data-demo="sampling" data-n="50" data-mode="se" style="width:70%;margin:0 auto"></div>

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Click "Draw 1,000".

The red bracket over the lower histogram spans ±1 standard deviation of the
sample means drawn so far. That standard deviation is the standard error. It
appears after two samples and settles as the draws accumulate; after "Draw
10" it is already $6.97.

Three numbers in the readout. The standard deviation of the 1,000 sample
means is about $7.0: the standard error, measured directly, which is
possible only in a simulation. The true standard error is σ/√n = $49.02/√50
= $6.93. The estimated standard error s/√n uses the sample standard
deviation s of the last sample; it varies from sample to sample because s
does, and its mean across the 1,000 samples is close to the true value.

The formula uses the variability within one sample to estimate the
variability of the estimator across samples that were never drawn. With a
skewed population and n = 50, that estimate is itself noisy, which the last
sample shows.

The square of the standard error is the variance of the estimator.

In a report: mean monthly spend is $71, with a standard error of $7. The
standard error is a property of the estimator, not of this particular
estimate.
:::

## The standard error falls with the square root of n

- For the sample mean, σ/√n holds when the n draws are independent.

<div class="m06" data-demo="samplesize" style="width:92%;margin:0 auto"></div>

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Click "Draw 1,000 samples of each".

The same estimator, the sample mean, at n = 25, 100 and 400. All three
sampling distributions are centered on the population mean. The simulated
standard deviations are $9.39, $4.61 and $2.44; the true standard errors,
σ/√n, are $9.80, $4.90 and $2.45.

Each fourfold increase in n halves the standard error. Halving the standard
error requires four times the observations. Dividing it by ten requires a
hundred times the observations.

The budget implication: doubling the sample reduces the standard error by
about 30%, not by half.

The bullet is the condition. The simulation draws customers independently.
With dependent draws, such as shoppers clustered in a few stores, the
standard error falls more slowly than σ/√n and the formula understates it.
Section 3 and meeting 7 return to this.
:::

## Why the standard error falls as n grows

- In a mean, deviations above and below the population mean offset each other.
- With population variance σ², the sample mean has variance σ²/n and standard error σ/√n.
- A poll of 1,000 has a 95% margin of error of about ±3.1 points.
- With 4,000 respondents, the margin is about ±1.55 points.
- Precision depends on the sample size, not the population size.
- This requires independent observations.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

The mechanism: one customer can be $300 from the population mean. The mean
of 50 customers rarely is, because large and small values offset. The
variance of a sum of n independent draws is nσ²; dividing by n² gives σ²/n
for the mean.

Here σ is about $49, and $49/√50 is about $6.9, matching the simulation.

The poll figure is the same formula for a proportion near one half: 1.96 ×
√(0.25/1,000) = 0.031.

The fifth bullet surprises most people. A random sample of 1,000 has
essentially the same precision for the United States as for Ithaca. The
finite-population correction is negligible whenever the sample is a small
fraction of the population.

The last bullet is the key assumption. Section 3 and meeting 7 show what
happens when observations are dependent.
:::

## What a 95% confidence interval means

- **Confidence interval**: the estimate ± 1.96 standard errors.
- [In repeated samples]{.underline}, 95% of such intervals contain the parameter.

<div class="m06" data-demo="intervals" data-n="50" style="width:82%;margin:0 auto"></div>

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Click "Draw one" twice, then "Draw 100".

Each line is one sample's 95% confidence interval: the sample mean ± 1.96
estimated standard errors. Grey intervals contain the population mean. Red
intervals do not. In expectation 5 in 100 miss; in this seeded run, 7 of
the first 100 miss, which is within ordinary sampling variation.

The 95% is a property of the procedure. Across repeated samples, 95% of the
intervals it produces contain the parameter. Any single interval either
contains it or does not, and you cannot tell which.

A useful reading for reports: the interval is the set of parameter values
consistent with the data at the 5% level. Section 6 relies on this reading.
:::

# 2. Properties of estimators

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. Three properties of an estimator, each visible in its
sampling distribution: bias (its location relative to the parameter),
efficiency (its variance), and consistency (its behavior as n grows). One
historical case illustrates all three.
:::

## The Allies estimated German tank production

- The Allies needed an estimate of monthly German tank production.
- Chassis, gearboxes and wheels of captured tanks carried sequential serial numbers.
- Economists estimated production from those serial numbers.

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}
| Monthly production | Serial-number estimate | Intelligence estimate | German records |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| June 1940 | 169 | 1,000 | 122 |
| June 1941 | 244 | 1,550 | 271 |
| August 1942 | 327 | 1,550 | 342 |
:::

[Ruggles and Brodie (1947), *An Empirical Approach to Economic Intelligence in World War II*, JASA 42, 72–91.](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1947.10501915){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Three minutes.

The parameter was monthly production of German tanks, all types. The
intelligence column is the combined US and UK assessment of August 1942
(Munitions Record No. 24), so the 1940 and 1941 figures are as assessed in
1942. It came from agents, reconnaissance and interrogations.

Richard Ruggles and Henry Brodie, economists in the Economic Warfare
Division in London, noticed that components of captured tanks carried serial
numbers assigned in sequence. The serials observed on captured tanks are a
sample from 1 to N, where N is the number produced. Their first report used
about 1,200 chassis serial numbers, with engine numbers as a check. Later
work used gearbox numbers, and the mould numbers on the rubber tyres of the
48 bogie wheels on each of two captured Mark V tanks.

After the war, the records of the Speer ministry became available. The
serial-number estimates were close to them. The intelligence estimates
overstated production by a factor of four to eight.

The table is on p. 89 of the 1947 paper.

This is estimation without regression: a population, a parameter N, a
sample of serial numbers, and a choice of estimator. The next slides compare
three estimators of N.
:::

## Three estimators of the same parameter

- Parameter: N, the number of tanks, with serials numbered 1 to N.
- Sample: five captured serials, 19, 40, 42, 60 and 88.

1. The sample maximum: 88.
2. Twice the sample mean, minus 1: 98.6.
3. The sample maximum plus the average gap between serials, minus 1: 104.6.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The logic of each estimator.

Estimator 1: N is at least the largest serial observed.

Estimator 2: with serials drawn at random from 1 to N, the expected value of
a serial is (N + 1)/2. Doubling the sample mean and subtracting 1 estimates
N. Here the sample mean is 49.8.

Estimator 3: the sample maximum falls short of N by about one gap between
consecutive serials, and the average gap is estimated by the maximum divided
by the sample size, 88/5 = 17.6.

A single sample cannot tell us which estimator is best. Every estimator
returns some value in every sample. Comparing estimators requires their
sampling distributions.
:::

## The sample maximum is a biased estimator

- **Bias**: the expected value of the estimator minus the true parameter.

<div class="m06" data-demo="tanks" data-k="5" style="width:88%;margin:0 auto"></div>

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. N = 300. Click "Draw one sample": five serials and the three
estimates. Then "Draw 1,000 samples".

The sampling distribution of the sample maximum has a mean of about 249 in
this run (250.8 in theory). The maximum can never exceed 300 and is almost
always below it. Its bias is about −50.

The first sample after Reset is 26, 138, 175, 269 and 299, giving estimates
of 299, 362 and 358.

Estimators 2 and 3 have sampling distributions centered on 300. They are
unbiased.

Bias cannot be seen in a single sample. It is a property of the sampling
distribution, so in a real project it has to be derived from how the
estimator works.
:::

## Estimator 3 is more efficient than estimator 2

- **Efficiency**: an unbiased estimator with smaller variance is more efficient.

<div class="m06" data-demo="tanks" data-k="5" data-impossible="true" style="width:88%;margin:0 auto"></div>

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Click "Draw 1,000 samples".

Estimators 2 and 3 are both unbiased. The standard deviation of estimator 2
is about 77; that of estimator 3 is about 50. With the same data, estimator
3 has the smaller variance. It is more efficient.

The reason: the sample maximum carries most of the information in the sample
about N. Estimator 2 uses only the sample mean and discards that
information.

The readout shows that estimator 2 falls below the sample maximum in 206 of
1,000 samples, about one in five (the exact probability is 0.20). The sample
itself rules those values out. An unbiased estimator can produce impossible
estimates.

Efficiency has a cost interpretation: a less efficient estimator needs a
larger sample to reach the same standard error.
:::

## All three estimators are consistent

- **Consistency**: the estimator converges to the true parameter as n grows.

<div class="m06" data-demo="tanks" data-k="5" data-ks="5,20,80" style="width:88%;margin:0 auto"></div>

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Draw 1,000 samples at n = 5, then switch to n = 20 and draw,
then n = 80 and draw.

All three sampling distributions concentrate at 300. The bias of the sample
maximum falls from about −49 to about −13 to about −3. All three estimators
are consistent.

The rates differ. At n = 80 the standard deviation of estimator 3 is about
3, and that of estimator 2 about 17. The standard deviation of estimator 2,
built on a sample mean, falls with √n: four times the data halves it. The
estimators built on the sample maximum have standard deviations that fall
with n: four times the data divides it by four. The rate at which precision
improves depends on the estimator.

Consistency is the minimum requirement for an estimator. An inconsistent
estimator does not converge to the parameter however large the sample.
Section 3 shows how that happens.
:::

## The median can be more efficient than the mean

<div class="m06" data-demo="medianmean"></div>

- Normal population: the sample mean has the smaller variance.
- Heavy-tailed population: the sample median has the smaller variance.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. A second comparison of efficiency, using estimators they
already know.

Left: heights, approximately normal. Both the sample mean and the sample
median of 25 observations are unbiased for the center. The mean has the
smaller variance. For normal data the median's variance is π/2 ≈ 1.57 times
the mean's, so the median needs about 57% more observations for the same
standard error.

Right: a symmetric heavy-tailed population, like daily stock returns.
Extreme observations shift the sample mean but not the sample median. The
median now has the smaller variance.

Relative efficiency depends on the population distribution, so the choice
of estimator requires some knowledge of the data.

A caution for skewed populations: there the mean and the median are
different parameters, and the choice between them is a choice of question.
:::

## The bias–variance trade-off

<div class="m06" data-demo="darts" style="width:44%;margin:0 auto"></div>

- **Mean squared error**: the expected squared distance between an estimator $\hat\theta$ and the parameter $\theta$.

$$
\text{MSE}(\hat\theta) = E\big[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2\big] = \text{Bias}(\hat\theta)^2 + \text{Var}(\hat\theta)
$$

- $\text{Bias}(\hat\theta) = E[\hat\theta]-\theta$ and $\text{Var}(\hat\theta) = E\big[(\hat\theta-E[\hat\theta])^2\big]$. The identity holds whenever the variance is finite.
- A biased estimator can have a lower mean squared error than an unbiased one.
- Prediction methods accept some bias to reduce variance.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

The four targets separate bias from variance. The expected squared distance
from the bullseye, the mean squared error, combines both.

The decomposition is an identity, not an approximation. Add and subtract
E[θ̂] inside the square: the cross term has expectation zero, leaving
variance plus squared bias. It requires the estimator to have a finite
variance; the sample mean of the Cauchy draws in section 3 does not.

For predicting a new outcome rather than estimating a parameter, the
expected squared prediction error has a third term: bias² + variance + σ²,
where σ² is the variance of the noise in the outcome, which no model can
remove. The trade-off in the last bullet is between the first two terms.

Regularized regression methods such as ridge and lasso shrink coefficients
toward zero. They introduce bias to reduce variance, and are judged by
out-of-sample mean squared error. Section 7 returns to this. The next slide
computes the decomposition for two of the tank estimators.
:::

## The mean squared error of two estimators

<div class="m06" data-demo="mse" style="width:92%;margin:0 auto"></div>

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The tank estimators from slides 14 to 17, with N = 300 and
five tanks per sample. Same draws as those slides.

Click "Draw one sample". In each panel, the dot is the estimate θ̂ and the
red segment on the axis is the error θ̂ − θ. The red square is built on that
segment, so its area is the squared error (θ̂ − θ)². The first sample is 26,
138, 175, 269 and 299: estimator 1 gives 299, an error of −1 and a tiny
square; estimator 2 gives 362, an error of +62 and a square of 3,844.

Click "Draw one sample" a few more times. Earlier squares stay as faint
outlines. The sample maximum's squares all sit to the left of θ, because it
never exceeds N. Estimator 2's squares fall on both sides and some are
large.

The top row appears after two samples. It shows the means over all samples
so far: the squared bias, the variance, and the mean squared error, as
squares whose areas add up. Bias² + variance = MSE is visible as area.

Click "Draw 1,000 samples". Estimator 1: bias −51, bias² 2,619, variance
1,772, MSE 4,391. Estimator 2: bias −4, bias² 15, variance 5,975, MSE 5,991.
The biased estimator has the smaller mean squared error: its bias square is
large, and its variance square is much smaller than estimator 2's.

The variance in the readout divides by the number of samples, so the
identity holds exactly in the numbers shown.
:::

# 3. What a larger sample does not fix

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. A larger sample reduces the variance of a consistent
estimator. This section covers the cases where it does not reduce the error,
starting with the best-known polling failure.
:::

## The 1936 Literary Digest poll

- The Literary Digest was a leading US weekly magazine, with a circulation above one million.
- From 1916 it ran a straw poll by mail before each presidential election.
- It had predicted the winner of every election from 1920 to 1932.
- 1936: Franklin D. Roosevelt, the Democratic president, against Alf Landon, the Republican.
- It mailed about 10 million mock ballots, mostly to names from telephone directories and car registrations.
- It is the standard example that a very large sample does not remove bias.

[Lohr and Brick (2017), *Roosevelt Predicted to Win: Revisiting the 1936 Literary Digest Poll*, Statistics, Politics and Policy 8, 65–84.](https://doi.org/10.1515/spp-2016-0006){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Context first, because few in the room will know the case.

The Literary Digest was one of the most widely read American magazines of
the 1920s and 1930s. Its presidential poll was a straw poll: the magazine
mailed mock ballots, postcards asking how the recipient intended to vote,
and counted the ones that came back. It was not a vote in the election.

Before 1936 the poll had named the winner every time from 1920 to 1932, so
its 1936 result was taken seriously. The magazine itself had noticed that
its polls drew too many Republican voters from 1920 onward, but the
Republican lean had not changed the predicted winner before.

The names came mostly from telephone directories and automobile
registrations. The usual explanation, due to Gallup, is that telephone and
car owners were better off than the average voter during the Depression.

Why this case: it is the largest poll most students will ever hear of, and
it was wrong by a wide margin. It shows that a sample of millions does not
fix a biased way of choosing and hearing from respondents. It also ended the
era of straw polls: the pollsters who called 1936 correctly, among them
Gallup, used smaller, designed samples, and modern survey sampling grew
from them ([Lusinchi 2012](https://doi.org/10.1017/S014555320001035X)).
:::

## The poll missed Roosevelt's share by about 20 points

<div class="m06" style="width:76%;margin:0 auto" data-demo="digest" data-poll-r="42.9" data-poll-l="57.1" data-vote-r="62.5" data-vote-l="37.5" data-poll-label="Literary Digest poll, share of the two candidates" data-vote-label="Actual vote, two-party share"></div>

- About 2.4 million people mailed their mock ballots back. Those replies were the poll's sample.
- The poll predicted a Landon victory. Roosevelt won 46 of the 48 states.
- Gallup predicted the winner with a much smaller sample.

[Squire (1988), *Why the 1936 Literary Digest Poll Failed*, Public Opinion Quarterly 52, 125–133.](https://doi.org/10.1086/269085){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

About 10 million mock ballots were mailed and 2,376,523 came back, a
response rate of about 24%. Those returned mock ballots were the sample. The
Digest's final tally gave Landon 57.1% and Roosevelt 42.9% of the two
candidates' mock ballots, and projected 370 electoral votes for Landon.

In the election, Roosevelt won 62.5% of the two-party vote (60.8% of all
votes) and 523 of 531 electoral votes. The poll's error on Roosevelt's share
was about 20 points.

The standard error of a proportion estimated from 2.4 million responses is
about 0.03 percentage points. The sample size produced a precise estimate of
the wrong quantity.

Squire used a 1937 Gallup survey that asked people whether they had taken
part in the Digest poll. Both the initial sample and the nonresponse were
biased. By his estimate, the flawed mailing list did more of the damage, and
the nonresponse flipped the predicted winner: had everyone sampled replied,
the Digest would have predicted a Roosevelt victory.

Gallup's final poll gave Roosevelt about 56% of the two-party vote, from a
sample reported in textbooks as about 50,000.
:::

## A biased sample converges to the wrong value

- A larger sample reduces the variance. The bias remains.
- May 2021: 250,000 survey responses a week overstated US vaccine uptake by 17 points.

<div class="m06" data-demo="biased" style="width:72%;margin:0 auto"></div>

[Bradley et al. (2021), *Unrepresentative big surveys significantly overestimated US vaccine uptake*, Nature 600, 695–700.](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-04198-4){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Draw 1,000 samples at n = 25, then at 100, 400 and 1,600.

The same population, two sampling schemes. The top row samples at random.
The bottom row samples only respondents, and each customer's probability of
responding is proportional to the square root of their spending.

As n grows, both sampling distributions narrow at the √n rate. The random
sample mean converges to the population mean, $67.81. The respondent sample
mean converges to about $83.6, a bias of about $16. At n = 1,600 its standard
deviation is about $1.5 and its bias is unchanged.

The standard error measures variability around the estimator's own expected
value. It contains no information about bias, so a large biased sample
reports a small standard error.

The modern case: Bradley and co-authors compare three surveys of US adults
with the CDC's count of first doses administered. The Delphi–Facebook
survey, with about 250,000 responses a week, overestimated first-dose uptake
by 17 percentage points in May 2021; the Census Household Pulse survey, with
about 75,000 every two weeks, by 14 points. The authors compute that
Delphi–Facebook's bias-adjusted effective sample size was below 10 in April
2021: its 250,000 responses were no more accurate than a simple random
sample of 10 people.
:::

## Heavy tails slow the convergence of the mean

<div class="m06" data-demo="running" data-mode="both" style="width:92%;margin:0 auto"></div>

- Extreme observations keep shifting the sample mean, even at large n.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Click "Observe 2,000 draws".

Left: the running mean of customer spend as observations accumulate. It
fluctuates early and converges to the population mean: the law of large
numbers.

Right: the running mean of draws from a Cauchy distribution. It still jumps
after 1,000 draws, whenever an extreme value arrives. The Cauchy
distribution has no mean, so the sample mean never converges.

Business variables are rarely that extreme, but many are heavy-tailed:
revenue per customer, insurance claims, box-office receipts, follower
counts. Their sample means converge much more slowly than the √n rule
suggests. Options: report the median, trim or winsorize the tail, or model
the tail explicitly.
:::

## Four problems a larger sample does not solve

1. Selection or measurement bias. The bias does not shrink with n.
2. Dependent observations. 1,000 shoppers in 5 stores are not 1,000 independent observations.
3. Little variation in the regressor of interest. Two price changes in three years.
4. Heavy tails. The sample mean converges slowly.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

1. Bias: the Literary Digest, the respondent sample, and any variable
measured with systematic error. A larger sample gives a more precise
estimate of the wrong value.

2. Dependence: shoppers in the same store share its prices, weather and
staff. The usual standard error formula assumes independence and treats
1,000 shoppers as 1,000 independent observations, when the effective sample
is closer to 5. The standard error is understated. Meeting 7.

3. Variation in the regressor: estimating the price elasticity requires
variation in price. Three years of daily data with two price changes contain
two informative events, whatever the number of rows. Section 5 shows where
this enters the standard error.

4. Heavy tails, from the previous slide.

For any large dataset in their projects, the first question is which of
these four applies.
:::

# 4. Models and estimation methods

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. The model is chosen according to the type of outcome. The
estimation method determines how the model's parameters are computed from
the data. Two of the three methods already appeared in the tank example.
:::

## The type of outcome determines the model

<div class="m06" data-demo="outcomes"></div>

- Choose a model whose predictions stay within the possible values of the outcome.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Four outcome types that appear in their projects.

House price: continuous and positive. Ordinary least squares, often on the
log of price.

Loan default: binary. The model predicts a probability, which must lie
between 0 and 1. Logit.

Complaints per store per month: a non-negative integer count with many
zeros. Poisson regression.

Monthly spend with many zeros: non-negative and right-skewed. The log is
undefined at zero, and log(y + 1) gives estimates that depend on the units
of y. Poisson regression estimates the conditional mean directly and handles
the zeros. [Santos Silva and Tenreyro (2006)](https://doi.org/10.1162/rest.88.4.641)
established this for trade flows (PPML);
[Chen and Roth (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjad054) analyze the
problems with log(y + 1).
:::

## Linear regression can fit nonlinear relationships

- "Linear" means linear in the parameters.
- Terms such as age² or log(size) let the fitted relationship curve.

<div class="m06" data-demo="curves" style="width:92%;margin:0 auto"></div>

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds.

A linear regression model is linear in its coefficients. The regressors can
be any functions of the data: age and age squared, the log of size,
indicator variables. Least squares estimates all of them.

In this simulated example, price declines with age and rises again for the
oldest, historic houses. The model linear in age misses both ends. The model
quadratic in age fits the curvature.

With a quadratic term, the marginal effect of age depends on the age at
which it is evaluated: b₁ + 2·b₂·age. Report it at a few representative
ages.
:::

## Linear models can predict impossible values

<div class="m06" data-demo="impossible"></div>

- Logit keeps predicted probabilities in [0, 1]. Poisson keeps predicted counts non-negative.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

Left: default (0 or 1) against credit score. Least squares on a binary
outcome is the linear probability model. It predicts probabilities above 1
at low scores and below 0 at high scores. The logit model's predicted
probabilities stay in [0, 1].

Right: complaints against staff on shift. The linear model predicts negative
counts at high staffing. The Poisson model's predicted mean stays positive.

The linear probability model is still widely used, because its coefficients
approximate average marginal effects well. Its predictions for individual
units are the problem. Two of this afternoon's cards depend on this.
:::

## Three estimation methods

1. **Least squares**: choose the parameters that minimize the sum of squared residuals.
2. **Maximum likelihood**: choose the parameters that maximize the probability of the observed data.
3. **Method of moments (GMM)**: choose the parameters that equate sample moments to the moments the model implies.

- For 7 purchases in 20 visits, all three estimate the purchase probability as 0.35.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The three methods behind almost every estimator in their
software.

Least squares uses the residuals: it selects the parameters that make the
sum of squared residuals as small as possible.

Maximum likelihood uses a full probability model for the outcome: it
selects the parameters under which the observed data are most probable.

The method of moments uses a set of moments, such as means and covariances,
that the model implies: it selects the parameters that make the sample
moments equal to them.

In the simplest case they coincide. For a purchase indicator with 7 ones in
20 visits, all three give 0.35. They differ in richer models, and the
difference is in how much each assumes. The next three slides take them in
turn.
:::

## Least squares estimation

<div class="m06" data-demo="leastsquares" style="width:84%;margin:0 auto"></div>

- Chooses the coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals.
- Requires no assumption about the distribution of the errors.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Move the slope slider, or click "Sweep".

Twelve simulated houses, size against price, generated with a true slope of
$10,000 per 100 square feet. The red line is a candidate fit. Each residual
is the vertical distance from a house to the line, and each blue square has
area equal to the squared residual. Squaring weights large residuals more: a
residual of 40 contributes four times as much as a residual of 20.

The right panel plots the sum of squared residuals against the slope. It is
a parabola. At the starting slope of 3 the sum is 34,573. The least squares
estimate is its minimum: a slope of 9.76, or $9,760 per 100 square feet, with
a sum of 12,515. Click "Best fit".

Software computes the minimum in closed form; no search is involved.

Use: continuous outcomes, and the default in most applied work. Consistency
of the coefficients requires that the errors be uncorrelated with the
regressors, but no assumption about their distribution. Distributional
assumptions matter only for the standard errors, and section 5 relaxes them.
:::

## Maximum likelihood estimation

<div class="m06" data-demo="likelihood" style="width:80%;margin:0 auto"></div>

- **Likelihood**: the probability of the observed data, as a function of the parameters.
- Requires the outcome's full distribution. Most efficient when it is correct.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Move the slider, then click "Find the peak".

The data are 7 purchases in 20 visits. For each candidate purchase
probability p, the curve is the likelihood: the binomial probability of
exactly 7 purchases in 20 visits. At p = 0.20 it is 0.055. It is maximized
at p = 0.35, the maximum likelihood estimate.

Select "Both". With 70 purchases in 200 visits the maximum is at the same p
and the likelihood is much more concentrated. The curvature of the
log-likelihood at its maximum gives the standard error: 0.107 with n = 20
and 0.034 with n = 200.

Use: when a distribution for the outcome can be specified. A Bernoulli
outcome gives logit or probit, counts give Poisson or negative binomial,
durations give survival models. When the distribution is correctly
specified, maximum likelihood is asymptotically the most efficient
consistent estimator. When it is misspecified, the estimates can be
inconsistent.

The tank example: if every serial from 1 to N is equally likely to be
captured, the likelihood of the observed serials is highest at the smallest
admissible N, the sample maximum. Estimator 1 was the maximum likelihood
estimator: biased in small samples, consistent, and with low variance.
:::

## Method of moments estimation

- Chooses the parameters that equate sample moments to the moments the model implies.
- Tanks: setting the sample mean equal to its expected value, (N + 1)/2, gives estimator 2.
- Least squares is a moment estimator: residuals have mean zero and are uncorrelated with each regressor.
- **GMM** uses more moment conditions than parameters and weights them by their precision.
- It requires only the moment conditions, not the full distribution.

[Hansen (1982), *Large Sample Properties of Generalized Method of Moments Estimators*, Econometrica 50, 1029–1054.](https://doi.org/10.2307/1912775){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The contrast with maximum likelihood is the point of the slide.

Maximum likelihood used the full distribution: every serial from 1 to N
equally likely. The method of moments used a single implication of it: the
expected serial is (N + 1)/2. Estimator 2 was unbiased and less efficient
than estimator 3, which exploits the full distribution. Weaker assumptions,
lower efficiency.

Least squares can be derived the same way. Its estimates solve the sample
conditions that the residuals average zero and are uncorrelated with every
regressor.

The generalized method of moments, GMM, handles more moment conditions than
parameters by weighting them, with more precisely estimated conditions
receiving more weight. Lars Peter Hansen developed it, and it was cited in
his 2013 Nobel prize. It is used when economic theory implies moment
conditions without implying a full distribution. Instrumental variables
estimation, in the designs meetings, is a special case.
:::

## Comparing the three estimation methods

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}
| Method | Chooses the parameters that | Assumes | Typical use |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Least squares | minimize the sum of squared residuals | E[Y given X] is linear in the parameters | continuous outcomes |
| Maximum likelihood | maximize the likelihood of the data | the full distribution of Y given X | binary, count and duration outcomes |
| GMM | equate sample moments to model moments | only the moment conditions | instrumental variables, structural models |
:::

- Stronger assumptions increase efficiency when they hold and cause bias when they fail.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

Read across the rows. The assumptions column is the trade-off. Maximum
likelihood assumes the most and is the most efficient when its assumptions
hold. GMM assumes the least. Least squares requires only a correctly
specified conditional mean.

For their projects: a continuous outcome, least squares. A binary outcome,
logit, or the linear probability model if only an average marginal effect
is needed. A count or a non-negative outcome with zeros, Poisson. A design
based on an instrument, GMM, which statistical software labels IV or 2SLS.
:::

## Interpreting coefficients in linear models

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}
| Model | Interpretation of the coefficient b |
|:--|:--|
| Y on X | one more unit of X: a change of b in Y, in the units of Y |
| log Y on X | one more unit of X: a change of about 100·b percent in Y |
| log Y on log X | a 1% increase in X: a b% change in Y (an elasticity) |
:::

- For log Y, the exact percent change is 100·(e^b^ − 1). Use it when b is large.
- Percent and percentage points are different units.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Say each row as a sentence with its units.

Levels: a coefficient of 12,000 on a water-view indicator means houses with
a water view sell for $12,000 more, holding the other regressors fixed.

Log outcome: b = 0.08 means about 8% more. The approximation 100·b is
accurate for small b. The exact change is 100·(e^b − 1): b = 0.5 corresponds
to 65%, not 50%.

Log on log: the row reads per 1% increase in X, not per unit. b = −1.8 is an
elasticity: a 1% price increase is associated with a 1.8% decrease in sales.

Percent and percentage points: a default rate rising from 4% to 6% is an
increase of 2 percentage points and of 50%. State which.

"Is associated with" is deliberate. Whether the association is causal is a
question about the design, meetings 7 to 9.
:::

## Interpreting coefficients in logit and Poisson models

- Logit: b is the change in the log-odds of Y = 1 for a one-unit increase in X.
- e^b^ is the odds ratio. It is not a ratio of probabilities.
- Report the average marginal effect: the change in P(Y = 1), in percentage points.
- Poisson: a one-unit increase in X changes the expected count by 100·(e^b^ − 1) percent.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

Logit coefficients are in log-odds, which have no direct interpretation for
a decision maker. Exponentiating gives the odds ratio, which is often
misread as a ratio of probabilities; the two are close only when the
probability is small.

The average marginal effect is the change in the predicted probability for
a one-unit increase in X, averaged over the sample. Every statistical
package computes it. Report it in percentage points: a coupon raises the
probability of purchase by 3 percentage points.

Poisson: b = 0.10 means about 10.5% more expected complaints per unit of X.
e^b is the incidence rate ratio.
:::

# 5. Standard errors

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. The simulations computed the standard error from thousands
of samples. In a project there is one sample. There are two ways to
estimate the standard error from it: an analytical formula, or the
bootstrap.
:::

## Analytical standard errors

- Sample mean: s/√n, where s is the sample standard deviation of Y.
- OLS slope: approximately s~e~/(√n · s~X~).
- s~e~ is the standard deviation of the residuals. s~X~ is the standard deviation of X.
- Maximum likelihood: from the curvature of the log-likelihood at its maximum.
- All three assume independent observations.
- Heteroskedasticity-robust and clustered standard errors relax this. Meeting 7.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

The first appeared in section 1.

The second shows what determines the precision of a slope: the standard
deviation of the residuals, s_e, the sample size n, and the standard
deviation of the regressor, s_X. In a simple regression the formula is
exact up to a degrees-of-freedom correction. With little variation in X, s_X is close to zero and the
standard error is large regardless of n. This is the two-price-changes
problem from section 3.

The third appeared on the likelihood slide: a more sharply curved
log-likelihood gives a smaller standard error.

Statistical software computes all of these. The default versions assume
independent observations with constant error variance.
Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors allow the error variance to differ
across observations. Clustered standard errors allow observations within a
group, such as a store or a county, to be correlated. Meeting 7.
:::

## The bootstrap resamples the observed data

<div class="m06" data-demo="bootstrap" style="width:88%;margin:0 auto"></div>

- It treats the sample as the population and draws n observations with replacement.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Click "Draw one bootstrap sample" two or three times, then
"Draw 1,000 bootstrap samples".

The observed sample has 30 customers. There is no simple analytical formula
for the standard error of a sample median. Efron (1979) proposed treating
the sample as if it were the population and resampling from it.

A bootstrap sample draws 30 observations from the 30, with replacement. Some
customers appear two or three times and others not at all. Compute the
median, record it, and repeat.

The standard deviation of the 1,000 bootstrap medians is the bootstrap
standard error: $8.20. The readout compares it with the true standard error,
computed from 1,000 new samples from the population, which is possible only
because the population is simulated: $8.19. The sample median is $52.13.

Reference: [Efron (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176344552).
:::

## When to use the bootstrap

- No analytical formula exists: medians, ratios, percentiles.
- The sample is small or skewed, so the normal approximation is poor.
- The estimator has several steps, such as a forecast built from two models.
- The data are clustered: resample clusters, not observations.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds.

No formula: the median, a ratio of two means, the 90th percentile, a Gini
coefficient.

Small or skewed samples: analytical standard errors rely on approximations
that improve with n and can be poor with 30 skewed observations.

Multi-step estimators: a profit forecast computed from an estimated demand
model and an estimated cost model. The bootstrap re-estimates both models
in every bootstrap sample, so the uncertainty from both steps is included.

Clustered data: resample stores rather than shoppers, keeping each store's
shoppers together. This is the cluster bootstrap.
:::

## The bootstrap fails for the maximum

<div class="m06" data-demo="bootstrap" data-stat="max" style="width:88%;margin:0 auto"></div>

- No bootstrap sample can exceed the sample maximum.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. Click "Draw 1,000 bootstrap samples".

The same 30 customers; the statistic is now the maximum. Every bootstrap
sample is drawn from the 30 observations, so its maximum cannot exceed the
sample maximum. A bootstrap sample includes the largest customer with
probability 1 − (29/30)^30 ≈ 0.64, and then its maximum equals the sample
maximum, $199.23, exactly. In this run 631 of 1,000 do. The bootstrap
distribution collapses at that value.

It would imply that the population maximum is known almost exactly, which
is false. The bootstrap fails because the parameter lies at the boundary of
the support of the data.

The tank problem has this structure. The standard error of estimator 3 is
available analytically. The bootstrap also performs poorly in very small
samples, and with dependent data unless clusters or blocks are resampled.
:::

# 6. Hypothesis tests and p-values

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. One experiment. The p-value is first computed by
simulation, then by the analytical formula.
:::

## A permutation test simulates the null hypothesis

- A/B test of a checkout web page: the old design against a redesigned one, 5,000 visitors each.
- Old page: 250 purchases (5.0%). New page: 300 purchases (6.0%).
- **Null hypothesis**: the page design has no effect on the purchase probability.

<div class="m06" data-demo="permutation" style="width:68%;margin:0 auto"></div>

::: {.notes}
Four minutes.

The observed difference in purchase rates is 1.0 percentage point. The
question: how likely is a difference this large if the null hypothesis is
true?

Under the null, the page a visitor saw is unrelated to whether they bought.
The page labels are exchangeable: the 550 buyers would have bought under
either page. A permutation test randomly reassigns the labels, 5,000 to each
page, keeps the purchases fixed, and recomputes the difference.

Click "One permutation". This is one difference generated under the null.
Repeat twice: small differences of either sign.

Click "10,000 permutations". The histogram is the distribution of the
difference under the null. The red lines mark the observed difference, ±1.0.
317 of the 10,000 permuted differences are at least 1.0 in absolute value.

That share, 0.032, is the **p-value**: the probability, under the null
hypothesis, of a difference at least as large as the one observed. The exact
permutation p-value, over all possible relabellings, is 0.0315.

Click "Show normal approximation". The curve is the sampling distribution
the textbook z-test assumes: z = 2.19, p = 0.028. The analytical test
approximates the permutation distribution.
:::

## Interpreting a p-value of 0.03

- If the null hypothesis were true, a difference at least this large would occur in about 3% of experiments.

::: {style="font-size:0.85em"}
- "*P-values do not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true, or the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone.*"
- "*A p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result.*"
- "*Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a specific threshold.*"
:::

[Wasserstein and Lazar (2016), *The ASA's Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose*, The American Statistician 70, 129–133.](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

The first bullet is the complete interpretation. It is a probability
computed under the null hypothesis. It is not the probability that the null
is true, nor the probability that the new page works, and it contains no
information about the size of the effect.

The quotations are from the American Statistical Association's 2016
statement, the first formal position the association took on a specific
statistical practice. The third quotation names business decisions
explicitly.

The 0.05 threshold is a convention. Evidence at p = 0.049 and at p = 0.051
is essentially the same.
:::

## What share of significant results are false positives?

<div class="m06" style="width:82%;margin:0 auto" data-demo="icons" data-ideas="1000" data-real="100" data-power="0.8" data-alpha="0.05"></div>

- The share depends on the proportion of true effects among the hypotheses tested.
- In online A/B tests, 8% (Airbnb search) to 33% (Microsoft) of tested ideas succeed.

[Kohavi, Deng and Vermeer (2022), *A/B Testing Intuition Busters*, KDD '22, 3168–3177.](https://doi.org/10.1145/3534678.3539160){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Three minutes.

Suppose 1,000 hypotheses are tested, for example 1,000 A/B tests, and 100 of
them are true effects. With power of 80%, 80 true effects are detected. Of
the 900 true null hypotheses, 5% are rejected at the 5% level: 45 false
positives.

That gives 125 significant results, of which 45, or 36%, are false
positives, with every test conducted correctly.

The p-value cannot reveal this, because it is computed assuming the null and
does not depend on the proportion of true effects among the hypotheses
tested.

Kohavi and co-authors report the success rates of experiments at large
firms: 33% at Microsoft, 15% at Bing, about 10% at Booking.com, Google Ads
and Netflix, 8% in Airbnb search. They count only significant improvements,
so they use a one-sided 2.5% level. With 80% power, the implied share of
significant results that are false positives is 5.9% at Microsoft, 22% at a
10% success rate, and 26% at Airbnb search. With 50% power, 9% to 37%.

For their projects: one significant coefficient among many specifications
tried is weak evidence. A hypothesis stated in advance and replicated is
strong evidence.
:::

## Intervals and the minimum relevant effect

<div class="m06" data-demo="sizematters"></div>

- Set the smallest effect that would change the decision before estimating.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The four rows.

Row 1: significant and large. The confidence interval excludes zero and lies
entirely above the minimum relevant effect.

Row 2: significant and negligible. The interval excludes zero, and every
value in it is below the minimum relevant effect. Very large samples produce
this pattern. Statistical significance is not practical significance.

Row 3: not significant and inconclusive. The interval contains zero and also
effects of 8%. The data cannot distinguish a large effect from no effect. The
appropriate conclusion is that more data are needed.

Row 4: not significant and negligible. The interval lies within the band of
negligible effects. This is evidence that the effect is too small to matter.

Rows 3 and 4 are both "not significant" and support opposite conclusions.
The p-value does not distinguish them. The confidence interval does.
:::

# 7. Prediction and causal inference

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. The distinction determines what an estimate can be used for.
:::

## Prediction questions and causal questions

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}
| Prediction | Causal inference |
|:--|:--|
| Will it rain today? | Does a rain dance cause rain? |
| Which customers will churn next month? | Does the loyalty program reduce churn? |
| How many units will sell in December? | What is the effect of a 5% price increase on units sold? |
| Which loans will default? | Does a lower interest rate reduce defaults? |
:::

- Prediction requires out-of-sample accuracy. Causal inference requires a valid comparison.

[Kleinberg, Ludwig, Mullainathan and Obermeyer (2015), *Prediction Policy Problems*, American Economic Review 105, 491–495.](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.p20151023){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

The first row is from Kleinberg and co-authors. Whether to carry an umbrella
depends only on a forecast of rain; the cause of rain is irrelevant. Whether
to pay for a rain dance depends on the causal effect of the dance on rain.
The two questions require different evidence.

Many business decisions are pure prediction problems: which loans to audit,
how much inventory to hold, which customers to contact. Those projects are
evaluated on out-of-sample forecast error. The causal questions require the
comparisons from meeting 2 and the designs in meetings 8 and 9.

The common failure is a project that builds a predictive model and then
recommends an intervention based on it.
:::

## Predictive accuracy is measured out of sample

<div class="m06" data-demo="overfit"></div>

- In-sample fit never decreases as regressors are added.
- R² measures in-sample fit. Out-of-sample error measures predictive accuracy.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes.

Left: 12 observations and two models. The degree-9 polynomial passes close
to every point, and its in-sample root mean squared error is very small.

Right: new observations from the same process. The polynomial's error is
far larger than the linear model's. It fitted the noise in the estimation
sample as well as the systematic relationship. This is overfitting.

Prediction projects therefore hold out data: estimate on one part, evaluate
on data the model has not seen. For forecasts, estimate on an earlier period
and evaluate on a later one.

R² is the share of the variance of the outcome explained by the model in the
estimation sample. It never decreases when regressors are added. A high R²
indicates in-sample fit. It does not establish predictive accuracy, and it
contains no information about causal effects.
:::

## eBay's ads were credited with sales they did not cause

<div class="m06" data-demo="ebay" style="width:74%;margin:0 auto"></div>

- March 2012: eBay stopped brand-keyword ads on Yahoo! and MSN.
- Organic search clicks recovered 99.5% of the lost click traffic.
- Other keywords: OLS implied a return above 4,100%. A randomized regional experiment estimated −63%.
- Ad spending predicted revenue well. Only the experiment measured what the ads caused.

[Blake, Nosko and Tadelis (2015), *Consumer Heterogeneity and Paid Search Effectiveness*, Econometrica 83, 155–174.](https://doi.org/10.3982/ECTA12423){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Three minutes.

Brand keywords are queries containing "eBay", such as "ebay shoes". eBay
paid the search engines to show its ad above the results for these queries.
In March 2012 it stopped bidding on them on Yahoo! and MSN and continued on
Google, which served as the control. Users clicked the organic link
immediately below instead: 99.5% of the click traffic the ads had brought
still arrived. The figure is a schematic of the paper's Figure 2.

Non-brand keywords: eBay stopped all non-brand search advertising for 60
days in 68 of 210 designated market areas, chosen at random. An OLS regression of revenue on
search spending, the kind of model that predicts revenue well, implies a
return on investment above 4,100%. The experiment estimates −63%, with a 95%
confidence interval from −124% to −3%. The effect was concentrated among
users who had not bought in the previous year; for frequent buyers, who
account for most paid clicks, it was close to zero.

This is the prediction and causal-inference distinction with a budget
attached. Spending and revenue move together largely because the ads reach
people who were going to buy anyway. The advertising decision depends on the
causal effect of the ads, which the predictive relationship does not
identify.
:::

## Claims and what the evidence supports

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}
| Claim | What the estimate supports |
|:--|:--|
| The effect is highly significant | The estimate is precise. Its magnitude is a separate question. |
| We found no effect | The confidence interval includes zero. It may also include large effects. |
| Our two million rows settle it | A large n reduces variance. It does not reduce bias. |
| Customers were 30% more likely to buy | Check whether this is a percent or a percentage-point change. |
| The model predicts sales very well | High in-sample fit. No evidence on the causal effect of any variable. |
| The standard error is tiny, so the estimate is right | The standard error measures sampling variability. It does not measure bias. |
